description: (UGEC1209 is double-coded with GDRS1001.)  This course aims to develop students’ ability to analyze the everyday life through the lens of gender. Drawing on the interdisciplinary nature of Women’s and Gender Studies, the course will guide students to examine how gender works as one of the primary social organizing principles in the movies we watch, the housework we do, the behaviors we express and many other daily activities that have been routinized. The first three lectures will equip students with a critical gender lens by questioning biology and getting familiar with theories of gender role, socialization, gender schema, doing gender and queer theory. All concepts to be explored in class will be explained with reference to research. At the end of the course, students will come to understand how political their personal life is. In particular, the course hopes to inspire students to take part in creating social change for gender equality, which is in line with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.
outcome: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to 1. recognize gender as a fundamental organizing principle of society; 2. describe how gender is constructed and in what ways it influences us at individual, national and global levels; 3. explain gender in various perspectives with sound justifications; 4. theorize cultural issues from a gender perspective 5. reflect upon their life and choices. 6. Consider changes in social practices and policies that can better address gender equality 7. Evaluate the barriers and challenges in achieving gender equality in diverse cultures

description: The course offers a more advanced exploration of key strands of feminist thought. Rather than reinforcing a static and often oversimplified portrait of feminism through the categories of first, second, and third waves, it invites you to engage with the debates that continue to shape contemporary feminism. We will examine selected foundational texts, appreciate their intellectual contributions and influence, and critically assess how far they provide us with tools to understand our present moment and envision meaningful social change in times of crisis. Students will read a range of works by theorists advancing diverse feminist perspectives and analyze the strengths and limitations of each. The course aims to familiarize students with the diversity of feminist theories and to introduce key issues on which feminists diverge.A blended-mode section is available for this course. Please refer to the “Class Notes” of that section for further details.
outcome: Upon completion of the course, students should be able to 1. state and describe the key issues and debates in contemporary gender studies and feminist scholarship; 2. understand difficult founding texts of feminisms and gender studies; 3. apply feminist theories to contemporary gender and sexuality issues critically; reflect upon feminist theories and formulate their own feminist perspective.

title: Quantitative Research Methods in Gender Studies
description: This course introduces students to quantitative research methods and skills in Gender Studies. Students will be exposed to a variety of quantitative methodologies, and recognize gender bias in the application of research methods. The course adopts a combination of lectures, class discussion, and analytical practices. We will go through the different phases in the research process of formulating research questions, designing measurements and hypotheses, choosing of methods for accessing sources, conducting data analysis, and writing reports. Students will develop the critical awareness of quantitative methods through discussion and application of research methods and be prepared to design their own research project in the real setting with the quantitative research methods they learn in class. They will be able to reflect upon the choice and application of research methods from a gender perspective in their own research.
outcome: Upon successfully completing this course students should be able to: 1. Learn basic concepts and procedures of quantitative research methods and understand the logic of quantitative approaches in social analyses and in Gender Studies 2. Construct quantitative research with appropriate measurements and methods 3. Present quantitative research findings in an appropriate form orally and in writing
syllabus: 1. Introduction    2. Research design: taking gender into consideration  3. Conceptualization from a gender perspective 4. Survey research and feminist survey research  5. title: Qualitative Research Methods in Gender Studies
requirements: Not for students who have taken PSYC2070 and SOCI3231.
description: The qualitative research methods are an essential skill in the contemporary world and are widely used in gender studies. Having the gender lens in qualitative research lends itself greater importance as it helps to uncover the mechanism and the intersectional social forces giving shape to forms of inequalities, identities, and communities. As AI and big data are the buzz words today to restructure the future work force, qualitative research skills are becoming increasingly important in a world that are gradually governed by machines. People are not satisfied with merely algorithmic associations but want to know the meanings, emotions, sensibility, and identities behind data. Qualitative methods in gender studies capacitate us to engage in deep reflection about the process, dynamics, and the deeper structure of the social world to come up with a better solution to many problems of inequality. Gender studies is an interdisciplinary field, but in this course, we will focus on the qualitative research methods used by feminist inquires in the social sciences. Students will be exposed to a variety of qualitative research methods from fieldwork to beyond. Epistemology of gender research and what is considered feminist research will be introduced. We will cover important qualitative cases and the associated ethical issues. In order to understand the process of applying qualitative research methods, students will apply the knowledge learned in class through designing and conducting their own mini qualitative research project. They will report the progress of their research in class through group presentations or assignments to receive constructive comments from the instructor and fellow students. Respect and tolerance of different voices are important to the course.
outcome: 1. Understand the fundamental concepts, process, and ethics of qualitative research methods  2. Learn about different types of qualitative research methods that are commonly applied in gender studies  3. Frame research questions and employ research methods suitable for the research 4. Becoming reflexive of the subject and researcher’s position in qualitative research 5. Design and conduct research by collecting and analyzing data  6. Develop the skills for writing and presenting a qualitative research proposal and research

title: Advancing DEI in Organizations
description: The past few years have seen a growing recognition of the importance of diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) in organizations. This course aims to introduce students to the tools and frameworks needed to approach DEI from a leadership perspective. Students will gain a deep understanding of the organizational, cultural, and intergroup contexts in which DEI initiatives arise, which DEI initiatives work and why, the drivers that motivate DEI initiatives, and the opportunities and barriers to building effective DEI initiatives in organizations. The course is designed to help students navigate diverse organizational settings more effectively, work within and lead diverse teams, and apply DEI frameworks to address organizational challenges. The course also provides students with the opportunity to critically discuss topics such as identity, discrimination, micro-aggressions, and equity in society, and how these themes relate to organizational issues of power, privilege, opportunity, inclusion, innovation, and organizational effectiveness. By the end of the course, students will have the knowledge and skills to be inclusive leaders and advance DEI in business and other settings.

title: Love and Intimate Relationship
description: (UGED3208 is double-coded with GDRS3004.)  This course reviews basic concepts, theories and research findings of romantic love and intimate relationship. Various aspects of romantic love and intimate relationship will be critically reviewed. Based on research from a wide range of disciplines including gender studies, cultural studies, sociology, psychology, counselling, media studies, among various fields, together with input from literature and popular culture, the course will cover major areas such as the following: how do we understand the notions of “love” and “intimacy” in the different social and personal contexts, what are the different stages in a relationship; the influence of cultural myths and social scripts; interpersonal processes within romantic relationships (such as attraction, social cognition, communication and conflicts, etc.); how social gender role shapes romantic feelings and behaviors; notions of equality and freedom within relationships; power and violence; intimate relationship across life span, etc. Students are encouraged to actively reflect upon their own life experience, to engage in critical discussions of cultural phenomenon through case studies, and learn to untangle the cultural myths, norms, and stereotypes that shapes our private lives and our society in general. Upon the completion of the course, students should demonstrate basic understanding of structure, functions, dynamics, and development of romantic love and other interpersonal relationship. The personal is political. As personal relationships are the most basic social relationships that makes up the larger network of social relationships, it is hope that students could use knowledge from this course as an insight to understand, develop, and improve the quality of their own interpersonal relationship, and would aspire to build a more open and equal society starting from equalitarian and mindful personal relationships. Through critical exercise and personal reflection on notions and experience of Love and Intimate Relationship in relations to notions such as power, diversity, equality, and freedom, the course engages directly with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 by engaging directly with the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality), 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institution).

title: Gender and Sexuality in Contemporary Society
description: (UGEC3203 is double-coded with GDRS3005.)  This interdisciplinary course introduces and examines gender and sexuality from a contemporary and regional perspective. Based on a cross-cultural perspective, we will read and analyze different meanings of gender and sexuality, and how these meanings are constructed. In a context of modernization campaigns and globalization processes, this course illustrates how gender relations and sexual politics are related with historical backgrounds, cultural heritage, market expansion, ideological shifts, and capitalist dynamics. The topics of gender and sexuality will be interwoven with that of migration, work, family, popular culture, mass media, and consumerism. The course will help students to understand issues of discrimination against women and girls, unpaid care and domestic work, access to sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights, and equal rights to economic resources, and to reflect on how to promote gender equality (SDG5 among 17 Sustainable Development Goals, SDGs, in the 2030 development agenda). Students will be encouraged to explore localized knowledge and living experiences of gender and sexuality, and to think critically about how to reduce inequality (SDG10) related to social systems of sex and gender.

title: Living Feminisms: Creating a Nonviolent and Collaborative Future
description: (UGEC3204 is double-coded with GDRS3006.)  Living Feminisms is all about how to put feminism into practice. Specifically, it is concerned with living out feminist consciousness in every step of making fundamental and lasting social change. With this in mind, Living Feminisms is not an exposition of feminist theories per se but an exploration of how social change effort would look like when we take up feminist consciousness that transcends separateness and duality. It explores the root causes that lead to the domination system that has plagued humanity for centuries, examines the possibility of having a fundamental and lasting social transformation that supports life of all, and takes a closer look at a few selected alternative practices such as restorative justice and sharing economies that hold out hope in times of crises. The course also equips students with practical knowledge of being a change agent, introducing some practices with feminist consciousness that transform limiting beliefs about social change, nourish resilience by taking care of social and political trauma, and cultivate need-based facilitation skills and leadership that help navigate conflicts in the process of making internal as well as external transformation. To put it in a nutshell, Living Feminisms is a course that cultivates change agents with feminist consciousness.Living Feminisms deeply resonates with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 as a blueprint for building a sustainable future by 2030. The course directly touches on alternative practices working towards the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality), 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), 10 (Reduced Inequalities), 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions) and 17 (Partnerships for the Goals).
outcome: Upon completion of the course, students will acquire both knowledge and skills of social change that are in line with feminist consciousness. Specifically, they will be able to explain the roots of the domination system and a series of factors contributing to its perpetuation, and able to make change by transforming internal and external resistance. Students will be empowered to take lead in change effort through collaboration with others and mastery of conflict transformation skills. Students will learn to appreciate making a sustainable future requires transformation in areas broader than the conventionally defined economic realm.

title: Understanding Masculinities and Social Change
description: (UGEC3229 is double-coded with GDRS3007.)  This course examines men’s diverse experiences as boys/men and public discourses and practices about masculinities. It will focus on how the gendered social order influences men’s actions and the way men perceive themselves, other men, women, and social situations. It will pay special attention to the exploration of the relationships between multiple dimensions of social relations and inequalities including gender, race/ethnicity, class, and sexual orientation. It will address issues including but not limited to: male socialization, boyhood, male body images, male friendship, male sexuality and fertility, men’s experiences as fathers, male aggression and violence, men’s commitments to work, men’s social participation, and media representations of boys and men in contemporary culture. It will also explore other forms and interpretations of masculinities, such as female masculinities and queer masculinities, and to investigate to what extent they post challenges to hegemonic masculinity. Students will be introduced to the latest developments and their global networks, and to evaluate the prospects for social change in how men may think, feel, and act otherwise.The course resonates with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 by engaging directly with the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions) through critical engagement with different discourses and phenomenon related to masculinities.
outcome: Upon completion of the course, students should be able to: 1. state the key issues and concepts in the field of men’s and masculinities studies; 2. distinguish the competing theoretical approaches to men and masculinities; 3. understand men and masculinities in a cross-cultural perspective; 4. recognize that social class, sexuality, race/ethnicity and age cut across the issues pertinent to men’s and masculinities studies; 5. comment on the strengths and weaknesses of various theoretical approaches to men and masculinities; 6. theorize contemporary social issues in relation to men and masculinities; 7. critically engage with inequality in society in relation to different modes and notions of masculinities.

title: Public Policy and Social Minorities in Hong Kong
description: (UGEC3228 is double-coded with GDRS3008.)  This course examines the social construction of minorities and the history of Hong Kong public policy towards them, including legal changes, social institutions, immigration policy, and political mobilization. Current debates in public policies such as anti-discrimination legislation, education policies of ethnic minorities, disciplining of youth and anti-poverty scheme will also be evaluated within this context. We will draw on an array of intellectual resources ranging from political economy, critical race theory, feminism, phenomenology and queer theory to examine issues about racial/ethnic minorities, the economically underprivileged, minorities with disabilities, sexual/erotic minorities, gender minorities and youth in light of the latest scholarly discussions on multiculturalism, pluralism and the politics of difference and social recognition.The course is relevant to the Sustainable Development Goals 5 (Gender Equality), 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions) with a focus on how public policy plays an important role in obstructing and facilitating the attainment of these goals.

title: Family and Society
requirements: Not for student who have taken SOCI2218[3222].
description: (UGEC3224 is double-coded with GDRS3009.)  This course examines issues revolving the family as a social institution in different cultures. It explores processes of how the family is constructed in different forms as it intersects with various social systems including kinship, marriage, class, ethnicity, religion, and political economy. Particular attention is paid to how family as a gendered construction, while being a basic principle of social life globally, exhibits great diversity as it shapes and is shaped by local histories, traditions, and state policies. In an era of globalization and transnational mobility, the ideology and practice of the family are rapidly changing, but there are simultaneously trends of reversion and localization. Students will read ethnographies and develop cross-cultural perspectives on classic and contemporary issues concerning the family, such as work and domesticity, motherhoods and fatherhoods, sexual orientations, reproductive technologies, surrogacy and adoption. Students learn to critically think and articulate about family issues, and will acquire enhanced knowledge and skills in reflexive thinking and positive communication, cultural sensitivity, and diversity and inclusion. The course is relevant to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015, in particular SDGs 5 (Gender Equality), 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions).
outcome: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to:  describe anthropologically the different forms of family and the reasons they exist in different cultures, and have a broad-base understanding and worldview of the diversity of human experiences.  engage in contemporary debates in relation to the definition of family, same-sex parenthood and reproductive technologies, and to develop skills to dissipate stereotypes and discriminatory practices regarding sexual orientations.  analyze issues surrounding domesticity and violence against women in different cultural settings, and investigate potential solutions for gender inequality and evaluate barriers to related problems in their own society.  reflect on and apply concepts of cultural relativism, and to analyze ethnocentrism and explore ways to terminate racial discrimination.  reflect on their ability and steps to take as change-makers and agents of justice and peace.
syllabus: 1. The Family: An anthropological perspective (SDG #5, 10, 16)  The family is often imagined to be a social institution with a set of values and relationships shared by everyone in society. This is far from reality. In this lecture we look at the definitions of family across cultures, and look at how family interacts with different social systems such as religion, political system and modes of production, and investigate how family values may differ in different ethnic groups and how they change over time. Concepts of cultural relativism and holism will be introduced.      2. Kinship and lineage (SDG #5, 10)  Kinship and lineage have played an important part in the political economy of society, in the past as well as in present time. In this lecture we discuss the commonalities as well as the differences across cultures, and look at the factors leading to continuity and/or change, such as urbanization, globalization, appearance of reproductive technologies, adoption, surrogacy, and changing values in sexuality.     3. Role of marriage in family (SDG #5, 10, 16)  This lecture looks at how marriage may or may not be related to family formation, and the role of marriage in society. In addition, marriage regulations and practices are highly related to gender ideologies. These relations exist in diverse forms and have transformed over time, for example as governments promulgate new marriage laws and as civil society demands for reform.     4. Domesticity and gender division of labor (SDG #5, 10, 16)  How was the idea “man are breadwinners; women are homemakers” formulated in history and how is it challenged in contemporary society? This lecture will discuss issues of domesticity and how gender division of labor at home is related to the gender division of labor in society. We will examine the roles of religion and science, as well as of the church and  government in the production of gendered social arrangements. Students will learn to identify systemic barriers to gender equality.      5. Violence against Women (SDG #5, 16)  Why are women the majority of victims of domestic violence across cultures? Why do many women choose to stay in abusive relations? In this lecture we look at the social and cultural factors that influence women’s decision to confront, escape, or endure domestic violence, and discuss how family and  ideologies and practices have played a part in the perpetuation of VAW in different cultures. Students will investigate potential solutions for VAW as a form of gender inequality.     6. Parenthood and socialization (SDG #5, 10)  Do all parents love their children? Do parents in different cultures raise their children the same way? Why is raising children in families with same-sex parents, single parents, and migrant parents considered problematic? If socialization is the way to reproduce socially acceptable individuals, what form, content, and means should it take? This lecture seeks to dispel the misconception that parent-child relations are natural and uniform, by looking at the diverse forms of parenthood and ways of socialization in different cultures.     7. Spousal relations: duties, affection, and intimacy (SDG #5, 10)  How is spousal relationship culturally constructed? What are the components of spouse-hood and how do they relate to politics, economics, religion and other social systems? Why do extra-marital affairs happen and how does society deal with it? This lecture looks at the ideology and practice of spouse-hood across different cultures, and asks what role it has in formulating the family as social institution.        8. Globalization, affluence and livelihood (SDG #5, 10, 16)  This lecture looks at global transformation processes and how they affect the family both as a social institution and as a network of related individuals. We look at how consumerism, social media, and converging values seemingly sync-ing familial structures and emotions across the globe, but at the same time noting how families in different societies, as they undergo globalization and wealth polarization, are torn by desires of economic growth and downward social mobility.      9. Transnational mobility and family (SDG #5, 10)  In an era of globalization, more and more people cross national borders for a better life, creating transnational families as family members live in different countries in the form of split households, or as individuals become members of family in a different culture. In this lecture we look at this growing phenomenon and discuss issues about acculturation, family relations and power dynamics, how affines and agnates create transnational communities, and what happens to those who are left behind in the hometown.     10. New kinship and alternative family (SDG #5, 10)  We will discuss how arrangements such as same-sex marriage, cohabitation, and polygamous relations would challenge conventional understandings of kinship and family in society. We will reflect on these issues in relation to contemporary debates on heterosexual normativity, monogamy, and same-sex relations.     11. Doing family in China (SDG #5, 16)  The concept of family has various levels of meanings in Chinese culture, and throughout Chinese history these have transformed in response to the needs and ideologies of the time. While Han families may share certain idealized views of the family as a social system, its practice is perhaps as varied as the number of families. Ethnic groups and Chinese overseas communities add to this complexity as their worldviews, religions, and socioeconomic environments acculturate thinking and behavior that differ from what is understood as Chinese core values.     12. Doing family in Asia (SDG #5, 16)  This lecture will bring together ethnographic cases in Asia to illustrate the interaction of different social systems revolving around the family. By comparing changes and continuities of family formation and relations in the region using a cross-cultural perspective, we are able to reflect on our own culture, and understand the pros and cons of the ideologies and practices that we are socialized in.      13. Family, power, and intersectionality (SDG #5, 10, 16)  This lecture discusses individuals’ multi-layered identities and how these intersect with family membership. We will examine roles, statuses and power generated from positions in the family, gender and ethnicity, at work and school, on the media and more. The multiple locales in which individuals perform their everyday experiences are examined holistically, which helps us rethink how seemingly “natural” behavior are really cultural constructs, and how taken-for-granted ideas of family membership shape our everyday lives, our life goals as individuals, and the regulations and resources that constitute society.

title: Being Trans: Understanding Transgender Lives in the Here and Now
description: This course is one of the first courses dedicated to understanding trans-ness and trans-hood grounded in lived transgender experience in the East-Asian, especially the Sinophone, context. Conceptualised and co-taught by a trans person, the course adopts a holistic life approach, informed by first hand trans-perspective, in examining different aspects of our cis-hetero-patriarchal society (among many other exclusionary structures such as ableism, racism, ageism, etc.) through trans encounters in the everyday. Starting with tracing the evolution of terms in relation to the transgender identity, the exploration would be followed by reflections of the origin of the idea of “trans”, namely that of transgression and crossing-over, as an act of going beyond binaries. When inspecting gender frameworks in the “non-West”, especially those of formerly colonized societies, we can see how different understandings and imaginations of sex, gender, and sexuality would yield very different identifications, and thus human possibilities. Following more conceptual reflections, the second part of the course would be focused on societal structures as lived trans experiences, ranging from more social topics such as design and access of public facilities, the omnipresence of gender as identifier in everyday spaces and institutions, legal struggle for rights and recognition, to more intimate ones such as natal family ties, romantic relationship, sexual explorations and expressions, and reproductive experiments.The final part of the course would be an exploration beyond, reaching out to situate transgender issues within a larger context of other movements for progress and equal rights. Drawing from his experience as the city’s most prominent trans activist and a transgender support group organizer for over a decade, the instructor will be guiding the students in a critical examination of important debates within and outside of the transgender and the extended queer community, inspecting in-depth the simultaneous solidarity and tensions among different groups, from the increasing polarization and politicization of different interpretations of Feminism, to questioning the “imagined community” of LGBTQIA+ comradeship in HK and abroad, reflecting on the standing of transgender persons and transgender issues in the here and now.  The course resonates with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 by engaging directly with the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions) through critical engagement with different aspects, discourses, and phenomenon related to trans identities and their life experiences.

title: Women's Narratives and Hong Kong History
description: (UGED3206 is double-coded with GDRS3011.)  This course will revisit Hong Kong’s history through the exploration of narratives documenting women, a group often made invisible in history writing, as social actors in the fabric of colonial and post-colonial Hong Kong. From elites’ households to squatter huts, from brothels, textile factories to convents and schools, from public housing estates, prison, government offices to LegCo Chamber, women of different generations and ethnicities have been active players, caregivers, breadwinners, and pioneers, contesting the prescribed gender role and identity in a patriarchal society. The course seeks to not only explore how they lived, or how their lives are shaped and reshaped by their own unyielding efforts but also the different times they inhabited, but also to see how their stories can find ways into narratives and representations, both fictional, historical, and autobiographical. Drawing from a wide range of historical, fictional, and documentary sources, images and oral histories, this course will introduce a multi-faceted history of Hong Kong with women as the focus of inquiry. Through lectures, interactive tutorials, group projects and self-study, students will learn to relate the personal to social, political and economic changes in Hong Kong. Through critical exercise and personal reflection on Hong Kong history and the role of women in it, the course engages directly with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 by engaging directly with the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality), 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions).

title: Engendering Chinese Cultures
description: (UGED3205 is double-coded with GDRS3012.) The Chinese Century witnesses increasing local, regional, and global interests on China. In this spectacular era, Chinese culture has become a mediation of China’s economic activities, political institutions, social dynamics, and ordinary life patterns. Gender, as a major building block of society and culture, provides us with an analytical lens to understand how diverse forms of Chinese culture anchor feelings, thoughts, and actions invested within and beyond China.Covering academic research, historical materials, and contemporary cultural productions, this course introduces to students selected issues including history and modernity from late Ming dynasty to the New China, popular culture in contemporary era, the cultural productions of sexual minorities, and, finally, the regional debates over gendered diaspora and Chineseness. As they participate in learning activities of the course, students will be gradually led to understanding Chinese culture from a new perspective. Furthermore, students will have a chance to reflect on long-held values and beliefs which they have acquired as members of this culture, or which they witness in the daily life of the community around them. While unpacking the complexity and nuances of Chinese culture from a gender perspective, this course resonates with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) adopted by United Nations, including SDG 5 (Gender Equality), SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities). Students reflect on their various values and concepts in daily life through this course, and become a global citizen with an open mind.

title: Experiential Guided Research
description: Experiential Guided Research aims at engaging students in research to prepare them better for their thesis projects and future studies and career involving research. More generally, this course is designed to offer students an opportunity to observe research up close and gain hands-on research experience by working as a member in an active research team. No lectures will be given. Students are expected to attend and actively participate in research/supervision meetings.

title: Minority Experiences in Hong Kong: Local Field Study
description: While Hong Kong is a unique city where people of different backgrounds mix, discrimination and segregation is however still a fact of life for many. This course provides opportunities to explore and understanding minority experiences in Hong Kong first-hand through local field tours. The overarching theme of the course is Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI), with a special focus on topics including minority identities, differences and assimilation, micro aggression, community organizing, and critical cultural intelligence. Other themes to be explored in the course include ableism and disabilities, aging, internal and interregional migration, rural identities, among others. The course is coordinated by the teaching staff from this Programme, and designed jointly with organizations, stakeholders, and experts from different background and fields. Centred on the lived experiences of different “minority” groups and communities in Hong Kong, learning activities of the course mainly consists of theme-based local field trips, designed to increase students’ local community connection and exposure, experiential learning opportunities, and broadening their understanding and imagination of the social and academic relevance, practicality, and potentials of DEI.

title: Interdisciplinary Seminars on Diversity, Equity and Inclusion: From Research to Practice
description: This course provides students with an unique opportunity to explore an inter-disciplinary and inter-faculty approach to understanding Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI). Scholars from various disciplines with specific interest in topics related to DEI will deliver thematic lectures about how the concept intersects with their respective fields, and how DEI plays out in a wide range of research. Apart from the inter-disciplinary lectures, this course also places a strong emphasis on learning from workers and experts working in the frontline, supporting and building communities, and creating positive social change. Combining the inter-disciplinary lectures with sharing of frontline experience, the course seeks to introduce students to the many faces and possibilities of DEI, both in research and in action, as well as their creative interventions and unexpected connections with society. Through critical exercise and reflection on notions such as power, diversity, and equality, the course aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 by engaging directly with the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities).

title: Advancing Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion in Organizations
requirements: Not for students who have taken GDRS2012.
description: The past few years have seen a growing recognition of the importance of diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) in organizations. This course aims to introduce students to the tools and frameworks needed to approach DEI from a leadership perspective. Students will gain a deep understanding of the organizational, cultural, and intergroup contexts in which DEI initiatives arise, which DEI initiatives work and why, the drivers that motivate DEI initiatives, and the opportunities and barriers to building effective DEI initiatives in organizations. The course is designed to help students navigate diverse organizational settings more effectively, work within and lead diverse teams, and apply DEI frameworks to address organizational challenges. The course also provides students with the opportunity to critically discuss topics such as identity, discrimination, micro-aggressions, and equity in society, and how these themes relate to organizational issues of power, privilege, opportunity, inclusion, innovation, and organizational effectiveness. By the end of the course, students will have the knowledge and skills to be inclusive leaders and advance DEI in business and other settings.
outcome: Evaluate the aspects of your identity and personal experiences that shape how you interact and engage with others, as well as how others interact and engage with you in organizations.  Explain how issues of power, privilege, discrimination, bias, equality, and equity influence op-portunity and effectiveness in organizations. Propose ways to make relationships across differences in organizations more effective. Describe current perspectives on the relationships among diversity and inclusion in global or-ganizations  Describe current perspectives on the relationships among diversity, inclusion, creativity, and in-novation in organizations.  Analyze a company's current approach to leading diversity and use content from this course to propose ways to enhance learning and effectiveness in that company. Become familiar with best practices and policies for creating more inclusive work environments.

title: Introduction to Diversity, Equity and Inclusion
description: Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) are concepts that are increasingly discussed in different industries as well as wider society nowadays. Why has DEI gained increased attention? Why do more people and organizations pay attention to DEI? What is DEI and why does DEI matter? What are the different aspects of DEI in society? How do we move from exclusion to inclusion? When do we know DEI is not lip service? What happens when different ideas about DEI clash? Is DEI ‘political correctness’? This course will take you through an exploratory journey about aspiring to strive for being inclusive – it is an exploratory journey because there will be many unknowns and inconclusive answers. The course aims to pay attention to both theoretical concepts as well as what concrete actions can be done at different levels of society when we strive for DEI.

title: LGBTQI+ Studies: Identities and social change
description: (UGEC3227 is double-coded with GDRS3021.)  This course critically explores the development of LGBTQI+ studies as an interdisciplinary field of inquiry. It traces how LGBTQI+ communities develop against the backdrops of social forces and social oppression. It analyzes the cultural, social and legal environments that LGBTQI+ people live with, in diverse spheres such as families, education, employment, health and the media. The discussions focus on both the structural constraints that LGBTQI+ people face, but also the agency and resilience they display. It explores the development of contemporary LGBTQI+ identities and social movements, as well as the politics involved. The course also asks how gender and sexual diversity is understood in different parts of the world in an era of globalization. Students are also exposed to different practices, policies and laws that are related to LGBTQI+ people’s lives.The Sustainable Development Goals vow to work towards a society where no one if left behind, particularly those who are most vulnerable and marginalized. In many parts of the world, LGBTQI+ people are historically amongst the most vulnerable and marginalized in society. This course will discuss the unequal treatment they face in cultural, social, political and legal systems and discuss how such inequality may be addressed.
outcome: Upon successful completion of this course, the student will:   - Students are expected to be able to debunk how sexualities and intimacies are shaped by larger social forces and therefore socially constructed.  - Students are expected to be able to analyze the social and historical development of LGBTQI+ identities and communities.  - Students are expected to gain an understanding of LGBTQI+ lives in contemporary societies from empirical examples in diverse spheres of life.  - Students are expected to be able to critically examine how sexualities intersect with other social categories, such as race, ethnicity, class, age and disability;  - Students are expected to critically assess social messages regarding sexualities and intimacies and question the extent to which they themselves agree or disagree with the conventional ‘definitions’ and ‘norms’ in society.  - Students are expected to be able to explore and assess different practice, policy and legal options that are related to LGBTQI+ people’s lives.

title: Gender Biases in Education and the Workplace
requirements: Not for students who have taken GDRS2004 or UGEC2672.
description: (UGEC3225 is double-coded with GDRS3024.)  Educational and occupational accomplishments vary dramatically among individuals and profoundly affect lives. Importantly, gender is among the powerful individual characteristics that affect people's experiences in educational and work settings. Gender shapes youths' experience and outcomes of education across the globe and across history. This course is designed to introduce to students, with a critical mindset, important contemporary issues at the intersection of gender, education and jobs. The topics address the role of gender in school- and related preferences and achievements, with a focus on social and cognitive approaches. For example, what is quality education (SDG goal 4) and why is it important to evaluate it with a gender perspective? Do men and women really differ in their abilities, and if so, by how much? Is personal interest a better explanation of gender imbalances in occupations? What are the ways that biases exist in education and the workplace, and how do teachers, parents, and employers contribute to gender biases (SDG goal 5)? Can gender equality in performance and hiring be improved by removing stereotypes? The literature will cover childhood, adolescence as well as adulthood in order to provide insight into the age-related changes of the gender issues. Particular attention will be paid to issues that relate closely to daily life, both local and international. Empirical evidence will be reviewed to illustrate the gender biases and substantiate the explanatory theories. Potential interventions to address gender biases in education and the workplace will also be discussed.
outcome: 1. Be aware of gender differences and similarities and gendered treatments in learning and occupational contexts in daily life 2. Be knowledgeable of the classical and latest research on gender in educational and occupational contexts and outcomes 3. Be more informed about the causes of gendered phenomena in educational and occupational contexts and how to deal with them constructively 4. Be able to reflect on how gender has affected themselves as a learner and achiever
syllabus: This course is designed to introduce to students, with a critical mindset, important contemporary issues at the  intersection of gender and education and achievement. Collectively, the topics address the gender-education nexus in academic, occupational, and social domains from childhood through adulthood. We will pay particular attention to issues that relate closely to daily life, both local and international. Theories and data will be drawn mainly from Psychology but will also come from other disciplines.   In terms of SDGs, the course is most relevant for goal #4 (Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education) and goal #5 (Achieve gender equality and empower the marginalised gender).   Major concepts and topics: 1.       Quality education and equitable workplace  Open discussion and review impressions on education and occupational contexts locally and internationally to assess if our current education is inclusive and equitable, and if gender equality and marginalization of gender are still pertinent questions in our society.  Why is it important to achieve gender equality and empower the marginalized gender? 2.       Gender differences and similarities in educational and occupational achievement  This topic includes questions such as: Gender differences is a topic that has fascinated researchers and is a topic of daily conversation. Do men/boys really differ from women/girls, and how? How big are the differences? Does it depend on contexts?  3.       Gender-related academic and occupational interests and goals Some argue that the gender gaps in academic and occupational outcomes may not be entirely the result of differences in ability or prejudice, but differences in the interests and goals of men/boys and women/girls. Are there gender differences in what people prefer as study subjects and occupations? What do men and women look for in their jobs? 4.       Gender socialization in schools In modern society, we spend almost ¼ of our life attending school. While a lot of gender socialization occurs at home, the school is also an important ground for gender socialization. What messages do schools and teachers send to students? How does sexism occur at schools and what interventions have been tested? 5.       Gender segregation at schools: The case of single-sex education Single-sex schools exist in many countries over the globe. However, few may notice that such institutional segregation of gender in the context of education has been a matter of intense social and scientific debate in the West. What are the rationales for the setting up of single-sex education? Do they live up to the tests of scientific studies? What are the possible consequences of gender segregation at schools? 6.       Motivation, stereotypes and engagement: Does gender matter? On the personal level, various psychological mechanisms may be at work to produce gender differences in educational and occupational achievement. What are some of these mechanisms? For example, how does stereotype threat and self efficacy theories apply to create gendered phenomena to make education inequitable? 7.       Gender biases in the workplace  Women’s status in the workplace has improved drastically over the decades. However, have we gotten rid of gender biases in the workplace? What are some of the ways that gender biases manifest in today’s workplace, personally or institutionally, explicitly or implicitly?  8.       Interventions to address gender gaps in the workplace If gender gaps still exist in the workplace, what can be done about it? For example, what interventions may be effective in narrowing the gender gap in STEM participation? Many companies have adopted a quota policy to increase their representation of women. What have research shown about the impact of having more women or just more diversity in groups?    The teaching and learning approach will be a mix of teacher-guided and student-centred activities. Lectures will introduce the background knowledge of each topic and review the required readings. Then, students will be engaged in active group discussions. Before class, students have to post intellectual questions concerning the assigned readings. They will also look for additional discussion materials (academic articles, news reports, blog posts, etc.) and share them in class during discussions and presentations. The teacher and tutor(s) will monitor and guide the discussions. Towards the end of the course, students will present a poster on a self-selected topic related to gender and education/achievement in a mini-conference, and write an essay on the same topic to conclude their learned knowledge and demonstrate their ability to critically analyse the topic.

title: Innovating the Future: Gender, Science and Technology
description: (UGEC3213 is double-coded with GDRS3025.) This course examines the gender dimensions of innovation and novelty. The key questions are: How/Why/What/When innovation(s) are gendered? We will discuss the fluidity and messiness of doing and undoing gender in innovation practices and meanings produced. Broadly defined, innovation refers to new ideas, new knowledge, new technologies, new designs, and creative practices with the goal to solve social or technical problems. Many innovations may seem gender-neutral but are inherently imbued with gender perceptions. The course will equip students with ways to apply gender analysis to decipher innovations and innovative processes. The course incorporates sustainable development goals (SDGs) on Gender Equality and Reduced Inequalities to become more discerning toward more sustainable practices to advance Industry Innovation and Infrastructure. Using case studies from the technology culture, the routine practices, and the emergent new economy, students will learn to untangle how gender intersects with the seemingly neutral artefacts of innovation and technology. The course further covers how emergent issues of diversity and inclusion, AI and information technology, social entrepreneurship and social innovation, and leadership style could reshape the existing relationship between gender and innovation to advance sustainability and social resilience.

title: A Screen of One’s Own: Women and Films
requirements: Not for students who have taken GDRS3214, UGEC3214 or UGEC3215.
description: (UGEC3214 is double-coded with GDRS3026.) This course examines the rich tradition of feminist film theory and provides students with an understanding of its main concerns and debates. Topics will include the key semiotic and psychoanalytic approaches of the 1970s-1990s, classic films which have inspired feminist debate, avant-garde cinema, local cinema, independent cinema, and postmodern cinema, as well as recent cinematic re-conceptualizations and exploration of gender and sexuality local and abroad. In systems of representation from fine art to mainstream cinema to advertising, women have been constructed and existed as spectacle or passive object “to-be-looked-at,” in Laura Mulvey’s now often quoted words. Following her trail, feminist critics turned their attention to mainstream films and popular media addressed to female spectators and exposed the contradictions within and between the notion of “women’s pictures” and the diversity of female experience. Local cinemas and independent creators also tell their own unique stories of women’s lives in dramatically different cultural contexts. Critics from other fields further complicate these images by examining them through lens including race, class, ability, queerness, and more.Mulvey’s groundbreaking analysis of gendered looking relations in classical Hollywood cinema has since generated numerous analyses of the place of women as spectacle or passive object in films “cut to the measure of [male] desire.” Critics around the world showed how different groups of women attempt to take control of their positioning through viewing or using texts in their own ways, and by creating their own. What happens when female-identified artists, audiences, and theorists look back, and seek to rebel against such cinematic traditions by experimenting with alternative visual languages and narrative tools? This course starts with the paradigm of narrative film analysis that Mulvey outlined in the 1970s and move on to explore a wider range of questions in feminist film studies, including spectatorship, authorship, popular culture, character stereotypes in genre films, self-representation, (g)local cinema, and new feminist media. Students would be introduced to trailblazing works by female filmmakers worldwide, special focus will be placed onto important works in Hong Kong cinema for critical examination and comparative studies. Through critical reflections on notions such as gender stereotypes, representation, power, diversity, and equality, the course engages directly with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 by engaging directly with the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities).

title: Media Representations of Minorities in Hong Kong
requirements: Not for students who have taken GDRS3026, UGEC3214 or UGEC3215.
description: (UGEC3215 is double-coded with GDRS3214.)  How do we understand the notion of “minority”? And how does “minority”, look like, in cinema? This course examines the rich tradition of critical film theory and provides students with an understanding of its main concerns and debates, concerning “minority” identities and subalternity. Addressing key discussions about media representations of “minority”, the course will look at the politics of representation and its impacts, both on- and off-screen. We will be looking at how media works to construct “the Other” in different contexts, and delve into important work which have inspired minority cinema, subaltern cinema, avant-garde cinema, local cinema, and independent cinema among other counter-movements, as well as recent re-conceptualizations and exploration of representations marginalized identities, positions, and experiences, local and abroad. This course aims to introduces students to cinematic representations of differences as a productive paradigm of identity politics. While cultural theorist Stuart Hall suggests that identity politics is primarily a representation politics enacted through ever-changing conjunctures of differences, black feminist scholars bell hooks remind us that the margin is an open-ended position to create inside-out and outside-in connections. To examine the representation of minorities is therefore to cultivate an ability to embrace the margins, which allows us to ponder how the construction of “we” can be opened to “they,” the differences. With its divergent forms such as video art, film activism, commercial cinema and film system as well as film festivals, cinema provides a powerful medium for such a task. The question asked throughout the course would be: what are the normative representations of minorities in different forms of cinema? At the production level, to what extent could “minority” artists and theorists rebel against such normative representations—with what alternative visual images and narrative tools? At the level of spectatorship and reception, what kind of reading strategy could generate alternative politics of the minorities? What happened when digital platforms intervene into such endeavors of the minorities?In the course, we will look at how socially marginalized groups, such as gay and lesbians, transgender persons, ethnic minorities, women in different stages of their lives, people with mental illness, teenagers, the elderly and many others are portrayed, and seek to expand their on-screen existence in Hong Kong media. In the exploration, we will engage with key questions in critical film studies, including spectatorship, authorship, popular culture, character stereotypes in genre films, self-representation, systems of media production, pro-sumer culture, (g)local cinema, alternative cinema, and new media. Students would be introduced to trailblazing works by “minority” filmmakers and media creators worldwide, and important cinematic and media movements that challenge the status-quo. Special focus will be placed onto important works in Hong Kong and Asia for critical examination and comparative studies. Through critical exercise and reflection on notions such as power, diversity, equality, and freedom, the course aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 by engaging directly with the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality) and 10 (Reduced Inequalities).

title: More Than Mother Earth: Gender as an Environmental Analytic
description: This interdisciplinary course invites students to critically examine contemporary environmental challenges such as the climate crisis, pollution, and extinction through the lens of gender. It explores how human-environment relationships are intertwined with gender relations. Through engagement with key debates and theoretical approaches, the course equips students to unpack and analyze these environment-gender interplay. Topics covered include a diverse range of conceptual frameworks (e.g. hydrofeminism and eco-criticism), macro- and micro-level practices (e.g. ecocide and carnism/veganism), and cultural productions (e.g. indigenous literature and ecodocumentary films). Course readings and materials are selected from both the Global North and South, offering students a comparative and global perspective on the ways in which the interplay between environment and gender manifests across different local contexts.

title: Talking Across Differences: Compassionate Communication in Action
requirements: Not for students who have taken GEWS2161.
description: Words can keep one another at arm’s length, while bringing people together. This paradoxical nature, coupled with the fact that we cannot not communicate, makes our interpersonal lives moderately challenging and, more often than not, a source of joy, fulfillment, and connection, as well as frustration, unhappiness, and even conflict. In the 1960s, having witnessed humanity's capacity for both violence and care, clinical psychologist Marshall Rosenberg sought to develop Compassionate communication (also known as Nonviolent communication) to foster love, truth, and courage. This model enables people to stay connected with themselves and others by identifying and expressing their underlying basic needs, even during times of conflict. Not only does Compassionate communication nurture connection, but it also provides various tools to shift the mode of influence from power-over to power-with in collaborative settings, contributing to a peaceful and inclusive future. In fact, Compassionate communication has been recognized by UNESCO as one of the best practices for nonviolent conflict resolution in both formal and informal education worldwide. As working with people from diverse backgrounds becomes increasingly common, the ability to communicate across differences is essential. This course will cover all the essential concepts, processes, and skills of Compassionate communication for both personal and social life. Through interactive learning in the form of role plays, demonstrations, and real-life scenarios, the course will cultivate students' awareness of their needs and their ability to authentically express themselves. Students will learn to listen with empathy, make life-enriching requests, apologize without self-blame, navigate conflict, hold difficult conversations, and facilitate collaboration across differences.
outcome: 1. Explain and differentiate the key premises, processes, concepts, and skills of Compassionate Communication, including observation, feelings, needs, and requests, in relation to everyday interpersonal and social contexts.2. Apply and demonstrate Compassionate Communication skills in structured exercises and real-life scenarios, including self-empathy, honest self-expression, empathic listening, and making life-enriching requests without demands.3. Identify, articulate, and regulate their own emotions and needs, and attend and respond sensitively to the emotions and needs of others, showing increased empathy and emotional awareness in interaction.4. Communicate and collaborate with confidence and care in difficult conversations and conflicts by co-creating mutually acceptable strategies, expressing disagreement without blame, and seeking outcomes that cater to the needs of all parties.5. Demonstrate openness and curiosity toward differences in values, identities, and communication styles, and integrate Compassionate Communication principles to work constructively with people from diverse social and cultural backgrounds.6. Analyze and evaluate real or case-based communication episodes (e.g. conflicts, microaggressions, or everyday misunderstandings) by identifying observations, feelings, needs, and requests, and by assessing the extent to which Compassionate Communication principles are embodied or violated. 7. Design and sustain a personal or collective practice plan for integrating Compassionate Communication into one’s daily life, studies, or community work, and reflect on changes in one’s attitudes, relationships, and communication patterns over time.
syllabus: CLASS 1The Basics of Compassionate CommunicationThis lecture introduces the origins of Compassionate Communication—developed by clinical psychologist Marshall Rosenberg in the 1960s—and outlines its key premises. Framed as a language modality that fosters dialogue, Compassionate Communication is contrasted with other common forms such as debate and persuasion, and its emphasis is placed on overcoming four common language patterns that hinder connection and understanding. Central to the approach are its four core components—observation, feelings, needs, and requests—which enhance clarity and strengthen interpersonal connection. Students will learn to clearly distinguish between observations and evaluations, feelings and thoughts, needs and strategies, and requests and demands, while cultivating a “needs consciousness” that forms the foundation for empathetic listening.CLASS 2The Power of Empathetic ListeningEmpathetic listening goes beyond the mechanics of hearing words; it involves immersing oneself in the speaker's emotional landscape, understanding their feelings and needs, and responding with genuine care and understanding. In this session, participants will learn to distinguish empathetic from non-empathetic responses listening, and the power of empathetic listening in transforming conflict to connection.CLASS 3Practicing Empathetic ListeningTuning into the inner world of another person is a skill that requires refinement through repeated practice. This session will provide students with four easy-to-follow frameworks for listening to others with empathy. It will also offer important advice on making empathetic guesses more colloquial and natural in daily conversations. In empathetic responses, we often ask questions to gain a deeper understanding of the other person's experience. This session will distinguish between the types of questions that strengthen connection and those that do not.CLASS 4 Making Life-Fulfilling RequestsThis week's topic focuses on making requests in Compassionate Communication, highlighting our interdependence in meeting needs through others. While making requests can feel daunting, the course examines how they invite contributions to our happiness and addresses challenges like fear of rejection and underestimating others' willingness to comply. We will explore barriers to making fulfilling requests and share strategies for clear communication to improve positive responses. The session will also cover handling unmet requests and understanding the needs behind a "no." The goal is to help participants feel more comfortable asking for what they need while remaining open to any outcome.CLASS 5Expressing Appreciation and Making Apologies Without Self-BlameExpressing appreciation is often recommended by relationship coaches as a relational lubricant. However, through the lens of Compassionate Communication, our usual way of expressing appreciation can sometimes take the form of judgment, even if it’s positive. The issue with judgment—positive or negative—is its static language, which can cast others, and even ourselves, in stone.CLASS 6 Troubleshooting: Clearing What Stands in the Way of Using Compassionate CommunicationFailure teaches success. In this lesson, we will address frequently asked questions and common pitfalls encountered on the journey of learning and practicing Compassionate Communication. Understanding the challenges we face can transform setbacks into valuable learning experiences. We encourage you to engage actively by asking any questions related to communication and its daily-life applications. Together, we’ll explore strategies to navigate these challenges, enhancing both your understanding and practical skills in Compassionate Communication. Your inquiries will help deepen our discussion and foster a supportive learning environment.CLASS 7 In-Class Mid-Term QuizCLASS 8Navigating Cultural Differences in Communication StylesThis week’s topic explores the intersection of culture and emotions within Compassionate Communication. We’ll examine how cultural backgrounds shape perceptions, expressions, and management of emotions, focusing on the differences between individualistic and collectivistic cultures. This session will discuss how cultures define ideal emotions, prioritize emotional expression or suppression, and the impact on mental and physical health. Additionally, we will consider how cultural perspectives influence emotional interpretation, whether through individual expression or situational context.Ultimately, the goal is to enhance our awareness of how culture affects emotional experiences and apply this understanding to our Compassionate Communication practice.CLASS 9 Why Can’t You Understand?!: Talking Across Attachment Styles in Intimate Relationships Intimate relationships can bring immense joy, yet they may also involve pain. Often, we find ourselves unconsciously re-enacting the attachment patterns formed with our childhood caregivers or yearning for the love we once lacked within our families. As a result, we may expect too much from our partners or give too little in return. This lecture bridges Compassionate Communication and attachment theory, helping you understand both your own and others’ attachment styles, and discover healthier ways to express yourself and to listen with empathy and care. Specifically, this lecture will address the following questions commonly related to intimate relationships:-    If I'm in a “situationship”, how can I confess my feelings to the person I love and confirm that we have mutual relationship goals?-    After dating for a while, my partner's passion seems to have cooled off. I feel lost and want to address the issue, but I am afraid to do so. What can I do?-    My partner is wonderful, but there is a habit that I find hard to accept. Can I ask them to change?-    Some say you should not expect anything from your lover because the more you expect, the more disappointed you will be. Is this true? If I still have expectations, how can I express them?-    I care for my partner, but their desire for intimacy exceeds my comfort level, and I feel a bit stifled. How can I communicate my feelings without rejecting their love?-    I've tried, but I don't think we're a good match. Is there a “nonviolent” way to break up?-    I'm in pain within my relationship. My partner threatens to break up whenever they're dissatisfied. I truly want to love wholeheartedly—do I have a choice?CLASS 10 Dancing with Conflict (I): What and Why?Conflict is an inevitable part of life, and while it can be intense and overwhelming, it also presents opportunities for growth and understanding. This week, we begin our exploration of conflict through the lens of Compassionate Communication. We will start by examining our own typical reactions to conflict and identifying our default modes of engagement. We will discuss how conflict arises from differing needs, values, and interpretations of situations, and how these differences can be opportunities to learn from each other. This lecture introduces the idea that all actions, including those that trigger conflict, are attempts to meet basic human needs. By understanding the underlying needs and values involved, we can begin to shift from blame and judgment to connection and resolution.CLASS 11Dancing with Conflict (II): 9 Skills to Navigate ConflictBuilding on our understanding of conflict, this week we will explore the practical application of the "9 Skills" of Compassionate Communication developed by Jim and Jori Manske. These skills offer a framework for effectively navigating conflict, beginning with the vital "Zero Step" of being present and self-connected. We will emphasize the importance of self-empathy in managing reactions and remaining grounded. The lecture will cover inviting others into dialogue, creating a safe space, expressing ourselves honestly, listening with empathy, making clear requests, and acknowledging different perspectives. We will also discuss using gratitude, feedback, and confirmation to enhance communication and understanding. By applying these skills to past conflicts, we aim to build stronger relationships and navigate difficult conversations. Ultimately, the focus will be on gaining confidence in using these skills in daily life for more compassionate and effective interactions.CLASS 12Collaborating Across Differences: Compassionate Communication for Team WorkCollaboration is widely regarded as an essential means and a long-cherished goal across various settings. In this session, we will explore the roles and types of facilitation, along with practical facilitation skills to enhance our collaborative efforts. We will guide you through the process of designing a meeting, including setting a clear purpose and desired outcomes, as well as selecting appropriate processes. Additionally, we will have a brief discussion on alternative decision-making systems beyond majority rule, which are more likely to address basic needs without creating opposition.CLASS 13 Harvesting Co-Learning Experience

title: Thesis I
description: This course is intended to be the first part of a sequence of two courses that form a capstone of a student’s study in the programme. (For the second part, see GDRS4010 Thesis II; no unit would be awarded if GDRS4010 is not taken subsequently.) The course provides an opportunity for students to undertake supervised study on a selected topic of interest. Students will be led to examine aspects of the selected topic, conduct a critical literature review and a systematic investigation of the topic they have chosen. Students are required to apply for ethics approval as applicable, collect and analyze data, regularly discuss with the teacher concrete findings in their research and submit written progress reports as scheduled by the teacher and submit a complete project report at the end of the term. Students will present their work in an academic mini-conference and also be assessed orally. The assessment will be based on the thesis document, the oral performance, and performance throughout the thesis process.

description: This course introduces gender as an analytical tool to study Chinese history from ancient times to the present day. It demonstrates how gender challenges mainstream historical analysis and explanations. The focus is placed on the changing meanings and practices of femininity/masculinity across time. Issues such as gender transgression, homosocial relationships, marriage, sexuality and reproduction will be explored, both to shed light on, and to question our familiar perceptions of China. By examining the interaction between historical context and gender politics, this course also provokes reflections on methodologies, sources and discourses.

title: Gender, Sexuality and Race in Political Issues
description: The course will examine the relationship between the development of gender and sexual identities and that of the contemporary politics mainly in, but not limited to, Asian societies. We will look into how the contemporary politics and gender structures in the regions interplay and produce racial identities through the lens of gender. For example, the Korean-Japan and China-Japan dispute over issues of comfort women in World War II; Gender activism in Gaza and Arab Spring, the female suicide bombers in middle-East, and religious right-wing movements in Hong Kong and Taiwan. Students will learn how to examine the issues of gender and sexual identities and how they are deeply embedded within the global politics as well as local social mores. Specifically, the course is divided into two parts. First of all, we will review the key theories of citizenship, war, democracy, nationalism, human rights and so on – through the lens of gender. Students are expected to learn the core theoretical debates and methods through reading key texts. The second part of this course will analyze these theories and debates through cutting-edge case studies. Topics will include comfort women, sexual violence in war, terrorism, female suicide-bombers and right-wing religious movements, human trafficking, grassroots feminist organizations, anti-war activism and so on. Students are expected to establish a more solid and critical range of views to examine these global issues and political controversies.
outcome: * The ability to raise profound questions about social phenomena.  * The ability to design research and analyzing a data to answer the question thus raised.  * The ability to research both local and global including but not limited to politics, economy and culture.  * The ability to analyze and possess the multicultural and interdisciplinary vision.  * The ability of social practice: to learn the implications of sociological research for social change, political debates and innovation.  * The ability to research the relationship between conception of peacemaking and social constructions of sexual and gender identities.  * The ability to research and analyze the role larger political and social conditions play in perpetuating gender based harms, discriminations and exclusions.

title: Internship
description: This is an experiential course which combines theoretical knowledge with real-life practices in community organizations. As one of the capstone options for undergraduate studies in GDRS, before the start of the second year, students are required to complete a three-month supervised internship in an NGO which partakes in gender and sexuality-related services or advocacy work. The course aims to provide students with an opportunity to put theory into practice, apply what they have learnt in Gender Studies to real-life situations, and critically reflect on theoretical issues through the experiences they gain during internship. Through practice, this course equips students with better knowledge of agencies working in the field of gender and sexuality, and the skills specific to their day-to-day operation and long-term development. Upon the completion of the course, it is hoped that students would emerge as mature and critical social actors who are well prepared to work with people from all walks of life and cope with interpersonal, organizational as well as occupational challenges in various work settings with integrity, responsibility and commitment.
outcome: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to 1. further integrate theory and practice by applying theories to the issues arisen from real-life situations and subjecting theories to critical reflection through work experience; 2. demonstrate their knowledge of agencies working in the field of gender and sexuality, and understand their roles by embedding them in the historical, social, cultural and economic contexts of Hong Kong; 3. work and collaborate with others as a mature and critical social actor, and manage various challenges and difficulties with integrity, responsibility and commitment.
syllabus: Learning Activities: • Students need to attend a pre-internship workshop and do goal setting via pre-internship proposal; • Internship starts from June to August during which students will be assigned to an agency in the field of gender and/or sexuality in Hong Kong, mostly likely a non-governmental organization, or a charity group; • Students will work for the agency for at least 8 hours per week over three months for a total no less than 150 hours; • Students need to keep a log of their work every week; • Students need to submit a final report of no less than 3,000 words two months after the completion of internship, reflecting on the experience of working as an intern, the connection between theory and practice, and the issues arisen from the internship.Apart from the internship, students would also need to attend thematic learning sessions consist of lecture, field expert sharing, and student presentations.Session 1: Understanding the landscape: key concepts, and different modes of intervention  Session 2: Theme: Supporting women Session 3: Theme: Gender and sexual minorities Session 4: Theme: Disabilities and accessibility Session 5: Student presentations

title: Thesis II
requirements: Pre-requisite: GDRS4005
description: The course is intended to be the second part of a sequence of two courses that form a capstone of a student’s study in the programme. Students will be led to examine aspects of the selected topic, conduct a critical literature review and a systematic investigation of the topic they have chosen. Students are required to apply for ethics approval as applicable, collect and analyze data, regularly discuss with the teacher concrete findings in their research and submit written progress reports as scheduled by the teacher and submit a complete project report at the end of the term.
